item.title: Robot chipmaker Huixi completes Series B financing led by Beijing AI fund
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Chinese robotics chip company Huixi Technology has completed Pre-Series B-plus and Series B financing, the company announced on October 22. The financing was led by the Beijing Artificial Intelligence Industry Investment Fund, with participation from the Beijing Robotics Industry Development Investment Fund, Hidden Hill Capital and other investors. Existing shareholders, including Shunwei Capital and Cathay […]
item.content:encoded:
Chinese robotics chip company Huixi Technology has completed Pre-Series B-plus and Series B financing, the company announced on October 22. The financing was led by the Beijing Artificial Intelligence Industry Investment Fund, with participation from the Beijing Robotics Industry Development Investment Fund, Hidden Hill Capital and other investors. Existing shareholders, including Shunwei Capital and Cathay Capital, also invested.

The proceeds will support development of a new generation of high-performance chips for embodied AI and accelerate commercial deliveries. Huixi develops the R1 AI system-on-chip and Huixi Embodied computing platforms, combining processors with software for model deployment, simulation and real-time control. Its computing platform is already used in AgiBot’s Genie G2 robots. The company said its total equity financing this year has exceeded RMB 2.5 billion. [PE Daily, in Chinese]

item.title: Audi reportedly seeks Huawei platform for next-generation A8 built in China
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Audi is in talks with Huawei about developing a China-specific version of its next-generation A8 using the Chinese technology company’s vehicle architecture, Germany’s Manager Magazin reported. The proposed model would be manufactured in China rather than imported from Germany, with key development work provided by Huawei. The discussions also cover other premium vehicles, including an […]
item.content:encoded:
Audi is in talks with Huawei about developing a China-specific version of its next-generation A8 using the Chinese technology company’s vehicle architecture, Germany’s Manager Magazin reported. The proposed model would be manufactured in China rather than imported from Germany, with key development work provided by Huawei.

The discussions also cover other premium vehicles, including an SUV, according to the report. Audi aims to use the partnership to support its Changchun manufacturing operation, with initial production targeted before the end of 2028. The companies have not finalized an agreement. The proposal comes as Audi seeks to strengthen its position in China’s increasingly competitive premium-car market. [Manager Magazin]

item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: ByteDance’s cloud platform Volcano Engine released Seedance 2.5 4K on October 23, targeting film and television production with higher-resolution video generation. The company said additional training improves the rendering of facial expressions, subtle movements and visual details. The model is currently available for trials by selected enterprise customers. A Draft mode allows users to test […]
item.content:encoded:
ByteDance’s cloud platform Volcano Engine released Seedance 2.5 4K on October 23, targeting film and television production with higher-resolution video generation. The company said additional training improves the rendering of facial expressions, subtle movements and visual details. The model is currently available for trials by selected enterprise customers.

A Draft mode allows users to test shots and refine storyboards with lower-cost 480p previews before generating a final 4K version. The model also supports 10-bit color and is designed to preserve image quality, colors and fine details when working with reference materials or editing existing footage. Some film-production and post-production companies in China and overseas have begun testing it. [IT Home, in Chinese]

The mixture-of-experts model has approximately 428 billion total parameters, with 23 billion activated per token. It supports text, image and video inputs and a context window of up to 1 million tokens. Designed […]
item.content:encoded:
MiniMax released the weights for its M3.1 Flash model on October 23, making the model available for developers to download and deploy. The mixture-of-experts model has approximately 428 billion total parameters, with 23 billion activated per token. It supports text, image and video inputs and a context window of up to 1 million tokens.

Designed for coding, AI agents and computer-use tasks, M3.1 Flash improves inference efficiency through sparse attention, quantization-aware training and speculative decoding. The release includes deployment guidance for inference frameworks such as SGLang and vLLM, alongside support for multiple chip platforms through FlagOS. The weights follow the model’s initial service launch on October 19. [MiniMax]

item.title: MiHoYo team open-sources GameScaling models that control games through keyboard and mouse actions
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: A research team involving miHoYo’s Honkai AI researchers and university collaborators has open-sourced GameScaling, a family of models that play games by generating keyboard and mouse actions from visual observations. The release includes eight checkpoints ranging from 800 million to 27 billion parameters, built through continued pretraining of Qwen3.5 vision-language models. The models use current […]
item.content:encoded:
A research team involving miHoYo’s Honkai AI researchers and university collaborators has open-sourced GameScaling, a family of models that play games by generating keyboard and mouse actions from visual observations. The release includes eight checkpoints ranging from 800 million to 27 billion parameters, built through continued pretraining of Qwen3.5 vision-language models.

The models use current and recent game frames, together with previous actions, to produce short sequences of controls. Demonstrated tasks include mining and crafting in Minecraft, combat and navigation in Doom, and puzzle-solving in escape-room environments. The project provides model weights, inference code and example programs under the Apache 2.0 license, allowing developers to study how training across different virtual worlds affects interactive AI performance. [GameScaling]

item.title: Desktop CNC startup CubiFab raises tens of millions of RMB to scale production
item.dc:creator: TechNode Feed
item.description: Shenzhen-based CubiFab has raised tens of millions of RMB in a new funding round from Nanshan Strategic Emerging Industries Investment and Longhua Capital, according to an October 23 announcement. The desktop CNC company will use the proceeds to scale production and deliveries of its first product, the CubiFab C1, strengthen its supply chain and expand […]
item.content:encoded:
Shenzhen-based CubiFab has raised tens of millions of RMB in a new funding round from Nanshan Strategic Emerging Industries Investment and Longhua Capital, according to an October 23 announcement. The desktop CNC company will use the proceeds to scale production and deliveries of its first product, the CubiFab C1, strengthen its supply chain and expand overseas sales channels.

The C1 is designed as a personal CNC workstation that enables users to produce metal components on a desktop. It integrates processing guidance and on-device monitoring to simplify tasks traditionally requiring separate design, machining and setup tools. The company’s team includes former employees of Intel, Apple, DJI, Anker and Bambu Lab, combining industrial-control experience with consumer-hardware development. [PE Daily, in Chinese]

item.content:encoded:
DeepSeek has completed a $15 billion private funding round, nearly doubling its initial target following strong investor demand, The Wall Street Journal reported on October 22, citing people familiar with the matter.

The Chinese AI developer is also accelerating preparations for a potential Shanghai listing early next year, according to the report. The financing would provide additional capital as DeepSeek expands its model development and computing infrastructure. [The Wall Street Journal]

item.title: Why This AI Startup Is Taking a Different Path From Wonderful
item.dc:creator: TechNode Staff
item.description: Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter. For businesses adopting AI, the question is no longer simply which model to use. It is also where AI should run, how much it will cost, and whether sensitive data can remain under the company’s control. PeakVision AI’s answer is to bring more AI […]
item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: This article was written by Lucia, a TechNode reporter.

For businesses adopting AI, the question is no longer simply which model to use. It is also where AI should run, how much it will cost, and whether sensitive data can remain under the company’s control.

PeakVision AI’s answer is to bring more AI work inside the enterprise. The system treats the task—not the individual app—as the basic unit of work: users state a goal, and AI agents handle the steps across a local computing environment.

From Research to an AI-First Enterprise Stack

Founded in 2024, PeakVision AI began with two obstacles to enterprise AI adoption: the difficulty of deploying the technology and concerns over data security, co-founder and CTO Liangyu Nie told TechNode.

In March 2026, the company established its Hangzhou headquarters and received RMB 15 million in government R&D support. It delivered its first enterprise systems and closed an initial funding round in May, followed by a second round worth tens of millions of yuan in August.

PeakVision AI is building an enterprise AI stack that combines locally deployed computing, FengKan AIOS, and AI-agent services. The system is designed around how agents complete tasks, rather than how people move among individual apps.

“You don’t need to download different apps. You just tell AI what you want in a chat box, and AI does it for you,” Nie said.

The startup’s central product thesis is that: enterprise software may increasingly be organized around intent and execution, not menus, files, and separate applications.

The company plans to open-source FengKan AIOS by the end of October.

Scaling Enterprise AI Through Hardware, Services, and Partnerships

PeakVision AI makes money from hardware, subscriptions, and customized enterprise AI deployments. Its wider goal is to turn project-specific work into reusable solutions for different industries.

FengKan AIOS supports third-party hardware, while PeakVision AI is testing a selective approach to its Skill ecosystem. Nie said end-user Skills, which may contain proprietary workflows, will remain untouched. More generalizable Skills built by partners and forward-deployed engineers could be released to the market.

The company is recently testing the model through an FDE academy launched by Shanghai Sixunited Intelligent Technology with Advanced Micro Devices (AMD)’s support. AMD provides computing equipment, technical toolchains, and project resources.

PeakVision AI also works with chipmakers early in product development to optimize performance and costs, including through a partnership with ChangXin Memory Technologies to reduce memory costs.

Competing for Small and Medium-Sized Businesses and Going Global

While enterprise-focused AI companies such as Wonderful serve large, often regulated organizations with AI platforms and deployment teams, PeakVision AI is targeting small and medium-sized businesses.

Nie said these businesses face the same challenges—cost, technical complexity, and data security—with fewer resources to address them. PeakVision AI uses lower-cost hardware from China’s supply chain to turn each deployment into a repeatable solution for similar customers.

“I believe small and medium-sized businesses around the world face the same challenges,” Nie said. “They have the same pain points as large enterprises, but one additional problem: they simply cannot afford to spend as much.”

The company is pursuing overseas opportunities, with distributor interest in the U.S., Israel, and Saudi Arabia, and is also exploring Southeast Asia, Latin America, and Africa, where local AI may appeal to businesses with limited or unreliable internet access.

From Finance to Manufacturing

PeakVision AI points to manufacturing and financial analysis as early examples of its approach.

At a lifeboat manufacturer, the company said its AI agents shortened a product-design cycle from one month to one week. At a yacht maker, AI-generated designs shifted engineers’ work from drafting proposals to reviewing and approving them.

The company has also developed tools for anti-corruption authorities to analyze financial records and for police to trace funds linked to fraud, according to Nie.

Beyond Automation: What Remains Human?

PeakVision AI aims to reach 80 to 100 enterprises across 10 industries by 2027, with longer-term ambitions to make FengKan AIOS a widely adopted enterprise AI platform.

Nie believes AI cannot replace human judgment but acknowledges that it could reduce staffing needs. As AI takes over more tasks, workers may increasingly focus on reviewing results and making decisions.

“For an employer, tasks that once required at least five people could be handled by just one,” Nie told TechNode.

Megawheels also ranked first in Japan and had 2 million users. Behind those numbers lies LEQI’s ambition to navigate foreign markets and build a lasting global business. item.content:encoded:
Editor’s note: A 2026 QYResearch report ranks LEQI’s Megawheels brand fourth among manufacturers in the global two-wheeled self-balancing scooter market. Megawheels also ranked first in Japan and had 2 million users. Behind those numbers lies LEQI’s ambition to navigate foreign markets and build a lasting global business.

The Last Two Kilometers

A two-kilometer trip can be an awkward gap in a city. Driving means traffic and parking; walking takes time, and public transit may not reach the door. Electric scooters offer another option, provided they are portable, reliable and easy to use.

That is the market Shenzhen-based LEQI entered when it was founded in 2016. Its portfolio now spans electric scooters, self-balancing vehicles, e-bikes, electric riding luggage and electric motorcycles.

The idea is simple, but the challenge is building products that fit local travel habits, meet regulatory requirements and earn the trust of riders in unfamiliar markets.

When Luggage Becomes a Ride

One of LEQI’s newer designs takes the concept beyond the conventional scooter. Its L3 Smart Electric Suitcase appears in the 2026 Red Dot Award: Product Design listings. It combines hand luggage with a rideable platform: a fold-out chassis and handle let the case function as a scooter, while wide wheels are designed to provide stability when riding or sitting.

A colored LED strip adds a distinctive touch, while sensors enable the suitcase to follow its owner and avoid obstacles, according to Red Dot’s description. The design was recognized for combining luggage with personal mobility.

The L3 reflects LEQI’s ambition to bring mobility technology into everyday products. For travelers navigating sprawling airports or train stations, it offers a potential way to combine luggage and transportation in one device.

The idea is part of a broader shift in personal mobility: bringing rideable technology into objects people already use.

More Than a Scooter Maker

Today, LEQI’s portfolio spans urban commuting, outdoor recreation and sports, with products ranging from e-bikes and electric riding luggage to high-speed electric motorcycles and dirt bikes. Across these categories, the company is building capabilities in electric-drive systems, battery management, sensor-based control and connected software.

Some of LEQI’s engineering expertise can be applied across its product range. Battery management and electric-drive systems, for example, are relevant to both scooters and e-bikes, while sensors and connected software can support different forms of vehicle control and interaction.

But shared technology does not mean one-size-fits-all design. A commuter scooter must be portable and practical for daily travel; an off-road motorcycle needs to handle demanding terrain; and a rideable suitcase must fit the constraints of moving through airports.

LEQI’s challenge, thus, is to adapt its core technologies to these different needs while developing products that work well in their own right.

What the Rankings Reveal

In 2021, LEQI established a global branding strategy, operating Megawheels and LEQI as two proprietary brands. The move formed part of its push into overseas markets, where the company sold through platforms including Amazon and eBay, its own website and B2B channels.

Additionally, LEQI ranked first worldwide in electric scooter shipments in 2025, and its Megawheels brand had 2 million users and ranked first in Japan.

LEQI has pursued overseas distribution beyond its home market, but turning overseas sales into brand recognition, repeat purchases and reliable after-sales support remains a challenge.

The Work of Going Abroad

Online marketplaces can help manufacturers reach foreign customers without building retail networks from scratch. Yet shoppers compare prices, range and reviews quickly, while established brands may inspire greater confidence about repairs and replacement parts.

Regulation adds another layer. Rules governing electric scooters differ across countries, affecting speed limits, road access and required approvals. Products may need different specifications to meet local requirements, and compliance does not end when a shipment clears customs.

LEQI has experience navigating these issues. In a 2023 review, German technology publication heise described the LEQIsmart A11 as one of the few Chinese scooters with Germany’s Allgemeine Betriebserlaubnis, or ABE, road approval.

Each market brings different requirements. Understanding local expectations and providing support after a sale may be as important to overseas expansion as the vehicle itself.

New Capital, Bigger Ambitions

In March 2026, LEQI completed a Series B funding round backed by Xiaomi Group and Shunwei Capital.

The funding would support research into higher-power-density electric-drive systems, AI-based real-time decision-making and adaptive control, and next-generation interaction systems. It also plans to accelerate overseas expansion and strengthen global supply-chain and distribution networks.

LEQI may see its next stage as more than launching new products. It needs the engineering, manufacturing and distribution capabilities to support them across markets.

The Test After Launch

LEQI’s story reflects a broader challenge for Chinese hardware makers: manufacturing and engineering expertise can bring products to market, but they do not automatically create global brands.

The L3 suitcase illustrates how LEQI is exploring new ways to combine mobility with everyday objects, while its scooter business provides an established product category. Whether these directions become a durable advantage depends on execution: products must meet local rules, perform as expected and remain practical to maintain.

Rankings and design awards can draw attention. Building a lasting international business takes something less visible: products that fit into people’s lives, backed by service that keeps them working long after the novelty wears off.

item.title: ByteDance’s PineDrama targets overseas growth with an ecosystem behind its free model
item.dc:creator: Jessie Wu
item.description: ByteDance is extending the competition in China’s short-drama market to overseas markets. According to Jiemian News, PineDrama, ByteDance’s overseas short-drama platform, is operated independently by a team within TikTok’s business division rather than by the team behind Hongguo Short Drama. Since its launch, the platform has seen sustained download growth and has entered the top […]
item.content:encoded:
ByteDance is extending the competition in China’s short-drama market to overseas markets. According to Jiemian News, PineDrama, ByteDance’s overseas short-drama platform, is operated independently by a team within TikTok’s business division rather than by the team behind Hongguo Short Drama. Since its launch, the platform has seen sustained download growth and has entered the top 10 on the iPhone free-app charts in the US, Brazil, and Thailand.

PineDrama’s rapid growth is driven not only by its free model, but also by TikTok’s traffic and ByteDance’s content supply ecosystem.

Unlike established overseas short-drama platforms such as ReelShort and DramaBox, which rely on paid viewing models, PineDrama has adopted the free-to-watch approach used by Hongguo Short Drama, monetizing its content through advertising.

TikTok’s traffic gives PineDrama direct access to a large audience, while its competitors rely more heavily on paid user acquisition through third-party platforms. This creates a gap in user acquisition costs and efficiency.

Content is another key advantage. Most of PineDrama’s short-drama producers currently come from China, and many have experience operating on Hongguo, Douyin, or TikTok. Meanwhile, the platform is also working to attract local overseas producers and expand its supply of original content.

ByteDance’s ecosystem also offers a relatively mature IP partnership model. Producers can obtain licenses from the platform’s content library or distribute original scripts independently. For production teams, established cooperation procedures can reduce the time and effort required to negotiate individual deals.

According to one producer, around 70% to 80% of the IP used in the AI-generated animated dramas made by their team comes from Tomato Novel, ByteDance’s online fiction platform. Compared with relying entirely on original scripts, established IP can reduce uncertainty in content selection. The platform’s tiered authorization system also gives producers a pathway to move from promising titles to premium IP.

When traffic, IP resources, and production capabilities form a closed loop, ByteDance is building more than just a short-drama app. It is creating an integrated system for content production and distribution.

At the same time, intensifying competition in China’s short-drama market is pushing more production teams to seek growth opportunities overseas.

One producer noted that computing power accounts for a significant share of AI-drama production costs in China, while paid traffic acquisition also requires substantial investment. On TikTok and PineDrama, some productions can attract considerable viewership without additional spending on promotion, and overseas revenue-sharing returns can be more attractive.

However, the revenue figures cited by individual producers reflect specific experiences and should not be taken as representative of the industry as a whole.

From its free viewing model and IP partnerships to its global content strategy, PineDrama is extending the short-drama ecosystem advantages ByteDance has developed in China to international markets.

The key question going forward is not simply how many downloads the platform can generate, but whether it can consistently produce hit titles and build a sustainable content supply chain and monetization model overseas.
